Bekanāṭa occurs only once in the Rigveda,^1 when Indra is
said to overcome all the Bekanāṭas and the Paṇis. The natural
sense, therefore, seems to be ‘usurer,’ the explanation given by
Yāska.^2 The word has a foreign appearance, but its provenance
can hardly be determined: it might just as well be aboriginal
as Babylonian.^3 Hillebrandt^4 thinks Brunnhofer is right in

Bekurā occurs in the Pañcaviṃśa Brāhmaṇa,^1 where it may
mean ‘voice’ or ‘sound,’ the sense assigned to the word in the
Naighaṇṭuka.^2 It is, however, possibly, like Bakura, the name
of a musical instrument. In the Taittirīya^3 and the Kāṭhaka^4
Saṃhitās the words Bekuri and Vekuri occur as epithets of
Apsarases, or celestial nymphs, meaning, perhaps, ‘melodious’;
in the Vājasaneyi Saṃhitā^5 and the Śatapatha Brāhmaṇa^6 the
variations Bhakuri and Bhākuri are found.
